newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FEATURE - In former breadbasket Ukraine, weather key to crop.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - In former breadbasket Ukraine, weather key to crop.

text.p: A year ago, Ukraine was hoping for rain to fall on its sun-baked grain fields, once the pride of the Soviet Union. This year, farmers are praying for the heavy downpours to end.

"If we have good weather conditions, we can hold our own," said Valery Furman, deputy director of the National Agrarian University research complex in Agrostantsiya, 100 km (62 miles) south of the capital, Kiev. "If it keeps raining, we will have problems."

His worries illustrate how the old Soviet Union's former breadbasket, already suffering from economic hardships and the collapse of its public farms, must perenially contend with a factor even less subject to its control -- the weather.
The problem can be severe in Ukraine, where low fertiliser use, inadequate fuel supplies and ramshackle machinery compound whatever losses are caused by the weather.
Last year's crop was hit by severe drought early in the growing season. This year's may fall victim to July's heavy rains which have slowed harvesting in the south.

"Much of the grain could spoil," said Leonid Zhyvotkov, director of the Myronivka Wheat Institute at the Agrarian Sciences Academy. "The technological processes we use are weak and not everyone has modern equipment to dry and clean the seed."
WEATHER ALWAYS A FACTOR

Nearly six years after independence from the former Soviet Union, Ukraine's farm industry has nearly collapsed, with the collective farm system brutally imposed by Soviet strongman Josef Stalin largely intact but lacking any modern input.
Still, government officials think the grain harvest will recover to 35 million tonnes. Some research groups see 39 million tonnes, all big improvements over last year's pitiful 25.4 million tonnes.
But analysts say those figures depend on the weather.
"We can't do it by hand," Zhyvotkov said, walking through fields of undulating yellow wheat.

"We have had above-normal rainfall in the first 10 days of July," he said, looking skyward. "There has been rain in the south and in the Lviv region in the west, and a cyclone in the western Volyn region damaged the corn and destroyed roads."
Soggy fields meant that as of mid-July, Ukraine had harvested only 2.82 million tonnes of grain, down from 4.87 million at the same time last year.
But crop yields for all spring grains rose to 2.85 tonnes per hectare (2.4 acres), against 1.96 tonnes the year before.

Western agricultural experts say weather will be the deciding factor in the stricken farm sector, which regularly produced 50 million tonne harvests in the Soviet era when government support was plentiful and never-ending.
Agriculture Minister Mykhailo Zubets has said Ukraine still forecasts a robust harvest despite heavy rains, which he said had rendered the soil damp enough to interfere with the harvest.
Spoilage of products is a common problem. Farms, lacking enough machinery, are unable to gather all the grain from fields and store it properly to prevent rotting in silos.
BARTERS AND STATE ORDERS
"Our own problems aren't going away, just as they aren't for the whole agriculture sector," said Furman.
His crops -- wheat, buckwheat, barley, oats and sugar beets, all sown over 1,000 hectares -- feed both his livestock and the ageing farmhands who till the soil.
Furman said workers had survived by barter and by filling the state grain order, which this year has been set at 5.5 million tonnes -- a practice the government may scrap next year.
"We trade sugar for oil, diesel and machine parts," Furman said. "Most of all we need pesticides and herbicides, but we have no money to buy them. This is our calamity.
"Our technology is also old, and we have to go begging for parts. We will pay for it with grain, because we have no money."
But he said his farm had shied away from getting involved with Western commodities traders which seek to buy grain in exchange for supplies like pesticides, machinery or cash.
"A company takes the supplies but then fails to get the grain," Furman said. "Some farms are in debt four to five years, and this could carry on for 10 years."
Grain harvest forecasts included 20 million tonnes of winter wheat against 13.4 million tonnes last year, and exports at six million tonnes from three million tonnes in 1996.
MODERN MACHINERY

About 100 kilometres down the road from Furman's farm, a driver prepared his bright red, second-hand Massey Ferguson combine to cut a swathe in a field of barley to determine if the grain was ready to harvest.
Mykhailo Voitovyk, head of the Mriya (Dream) collective farm, borrowed the machine from a neighbouring farm.
Standing on the fertile black earth which the agriculture sector hopes will once again make Ukraine a breadbasket, Voitovyk said he was eager to harvest his 500 hectares but rain was stopping him.
"The rain could be really damaging, and is really slowing things down," he said.
Ukraine, which sowed 13.51 million hectares to spring grain from 1996's 13.12 million, has not forecast barley output. But officials say it will improve on last year's 5.7 million tonnes.
The government has been working to plant more winter wheat, more suitable to Ukraine's climate better than spring varieties, which are harvested eight to 10 days after winter wheat is cut.
Private farmers have planted 4.66 million hectares with spring grain this year. Government support for the sector has been scant despite repeated promises to implement market reforms.
